title: The Promise
text:
All the gold in the world seemed

dissolved into the luminous afternoon!

Barely a rose-colored dusk

tinged the chalice of the trees.


An unforeseen love joined my hand

to yours, dark and trembling.

We were Boaz and Ruth before the lovely

threshing floor that circled the farmhouse!


“Will you love me?” you murmured. Slow and grave,

the gentle promise of the sweet,

loving Moabite trembled on my lips.


And like an “amen” at that instant came

the call to prayer, raised in resonance

by the rhythmic bell of the hermitage.
editorial_note: The biblical Ruth imagery and the rural Angelus remain central; era is rendered as threshing floor, not epoch.

title: Reconquest
text:
I do not know from where the longing returned

to sing again as in the time

when I held heaven in my fist

and thought was a blue pearl.


From a mourning cloud, lightning—

a sudden fish—split the warm night,

and in me opened once again the chrysalis

of winged verse and its burnished star.


Now it is the glittering fennel

that raises toward God the mighty offering

of its burnished diamond lance.


The unity of light upon the rose.

And once again the dazzling conquest

of eternal poetry, victorious.
editorial_note: Hino is read as fennel, preserving the plant's bright spear and the poem's organic rebirth.

title: Like One Desperate Flower
text:
I love him with blood, with bone,

with the seeing eye and breath,

with the brow that bends thought down,

with this hot, imprisoned heart;


with the fatally obsessive dream

of this love that fills all feeling,

from the brief laugh to the lament,

from the bewitched wound to its kiss.


My life pays tribute to his life,

whether it seems tumultuous or solitary,

like one desperate flower.


It depends upon him as the orchid

on the hard branch, or ivy on the wall,

lifted, breathing only there.
editorial_note: The bodily litany remains forceful; tributaria keeps the unequal economy of devotion.

title: I Give You My Naked Soul
text:
I give you my naked soul,

like a statue no fine veil shields.


Naked with the pure shamelessness

of a fruit, a star, or a flower;

of all those things that possess

the infinite serenity of Eve before the curse.


Of all those things—

fruits, stars, and roses—

unashamed of sex without a covering,

for whom no one would dare fashion clothes.


Unveiled, like the body of a serene goddess

with the intense whiteness of a lily!


Naked, thrown entirely open,

by the longing to love!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the prelapsarian body and the speaker's movement from exposure toward active desire.

title: Wild Root
text:
Fixed in my eyes remains

the vision of that wagon of wheat

that crossed, creaking and heavy,

sowing the straight road with ears of grain.


Do not expect me to laugh now!

You do not know the deep memories

in which I am absorbed!


From the depths of my soul rises

the taste of pitanga to my lips.

My brown skin still holds

some nameless fragrance of stacked wheat.


Oh, I would like to take you with me

to sleep one night in the fields,

and in your arms pass into day

beneath a tree's unruly roof!


I am the same wild girl

you brought to your side years ago.
editorial_note: Pitanga remains untranslated as a regional sensory anchor; the rural memory keeps its erotic and autobiographical force.
